interviewQuestions.question: How do you structure your practice in the weeks leading up to a coding interview?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I work backward from the interview date and deliberately vary the mode of practice rather than doing the same thing every day. Early on, I lean toward untimed, pattern-by-pattern practice — the goal there is learning the mechanism of a technique I'm weak on, like interval problems, not performing under pressure yet. As the date gets closer, I shift to timed practice on a mixed, unlabeled set of problems, so pattern recognition itself gets exercised rather than knowing in advance which technique to reach for.

In the final week or two, I weight practice toward full mock interviews and genuinely cold problems under real interview conditions — no advance signal on the pattern, a visible clock, and someone actually watching. That stage is the one people avoid longest because it's uncomfortable, but it's also the closest simulation of the real thing, so I make sure I'm not saving it entirely for the last couple of days.

I also keep a short log of what specifically goes wrong on each miss, and I review it every week or two — that turns "I keep failing DP" into a concrete, addressable gap I can target directly instead of just doing more of the same undirected practice.

**Testing:** whether your practice plan actually resembles the real interview by the end, not just accumulates volume in the easiest mode.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Structuring a multi-week practice plan

interviewQuestions.question: Why doesn't solving a large number of problems untimed at home reliably prepare you for a live interview?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Untimed solo practice removes exactly the pressures that determine real interview performance: a visible clock, a live person evaluating your narration in real time, and the social cost of going quiet or looking stuck. Someone can solve two hundred problems this way and still freeze the first time all three of those are present together, because that specific combination — pressure, narration, observation — was simply never rehearsed.

That doesn't make untimed practice worthless; it's the right mode for actually learning a new pattern for the first time, when the goal is understanding the mechanism, not performing it live. The mistake is treating volume in that comfortable mode as sufficient preparation for the live, timed, watched version, and never practicing the version that actually resembles the real thing until the interview itself.

Concretely, I'd expect someone who only ever practiced untimed to under-narrate in a real round — since narrating live to an evaluator is a distinct skill from silently solving a problem — and to be thrown by a visible countdown they've never had to manage before.

**Testing:** whether you understand that practice fidelity to the real conditions matters more than raw problem count.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why volume alone doesn't transfer

interviewQuestions.question: How do you get useful feedback out of a mock interview, both giving it and receiving it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
As the person giving feedback, I keep it tied to a specific moment rather than a general impression — "at around minute 12 you started coding before finishing your stated approach" is something the other person can act on directly, while "you seemed a bit unclear" gives them nothing concrete to change. I take rough time-stamped notes during the mock itself rather than trying to reconstruct impressions afterward from memory, since memory tends to smooth over the specific moments that actually mattered.

As the person receiving feedback, the harder discipline is not explaining it away — resisting "I was going to say that next" or "I know, I just ran out of time." The interviewer's live read is the actual data point, because a real interviewer forms their impression without the benefit of your intended next sentence, so litigating it after the fact defeats the purpose of the exercise. I ask directly for the two or three things that would have moved the needle most, rather than a full list of every minor observation, since that's what's actually actionable before the next mock.

I also review a recording occasionally, muted, watching only pacing and body language — it's easier to catch that I looked frozen or rushed when I'm not simultaneously following the content.

**Testing:** whether you can extract specific, actionable signal from practice feedback instead of treating it as a pass/fail verdict to defend against.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Extracting useful feedback
